title: No One Can Afford to Make ‘Myst’ Games Anymore
gist: Cyan Worlds built a fully playable demo of a new Myst-franchise game (codenamed Anglerfish), pitched more than a dozen publishers at GDC and D.I.C.E. for a $1M–$10M finishing round, got positive reviews but zero money, shelved the project and laid off 12 people — roughly half its staff. The article uses that failure to document a barbell collapse in game funding: venture capital into gaming fell from a $12B 2021 peak to under $3B in both 2023 and 2024 after the Fed benchmark passed 5 percent, leaving the $2M–$15M double-A tier stranded between $200M+ triple-A productions and sub-$1M micro-indies, with Steam discovery simultaneously degraded by 18,000+ AI-disclosed titles.

insights.claim: Venture capital funding for the video game industry collapsed by more than 75 percent, from a 2021 peak of $12 billion to less than $3 billion in both 2023 and 2024, following the Fed benchmark rate surging past 5 percent in 2023.
insights.speaker: Adam Morgan
insights.so_what: Gaming content supply on a 3-5 year lag is set by the 2023-2024 funding trough — expect a thin release slate of mid-budget titles through 2027 regardless of demand.
insights.locator: So where did all the funding go?

insights.claim: The two prior booms in game-studio risk capital both coincided with near-zero interest rates — post-Great-Recession and the peak of the Covid pandemic — making the sector's project financing an explicit duration bet on cheap money rather than on content demand.
insights.speaker: Adam Morgan
insights.so_what: Treat game-studio formation and greenlight rates as a rate-sensitive cyclical, not a secular growth story; any easing cycle should be the leading indicator for a mid-budget greenlight recovery.
insights.locator: So where did all the funding go?

insights.claim: Publishers responded to expensive capital by rationing rather than reallocating — treating existing cash as fixed until bank rates change and deliberately stretching it, which suppresses greenlights even for projects their own staff champion.
insights.speaker: Adam Morgan
insights.so_what: Publisher slate cuts are a balance-sheet decision, not a quality judgment; positive internal reception is no longer predictive of funding.
insights.quote: Publishers looked at their capital and said, ‘This is all the cash we have until the banks change their rates. Let's be conservative and stretch this out.’
insights.locator: Money just got too expensive to borrow

insights.claim: Game financing has barbelled into $200M+ triple-A productions from studios like Rockstar, Naughty Dog and Bungie at one end and sub-$1M micro-indies at the other, with the $2M–$15M band now described as very difficult for most developers to finance.
insights.speaker: Adam Morgan
insights.so_what: The double-A tier is the structural short in interactive entertainment; capital deployed there faces no competition but also no exit path through traditional publishers.
insights.quote: The space between $2 million to $15 million has become very difficult for most developers,
insights.locator: In between the triple-A and micro-indie extremes

insights.claim: The subsidy that sustained the mid-budget tier was platform money — Xbox Game Pass and PlayStation alongside publisher funding — and most publishers have since pivoted toward much smaller budgets, removing the prop rather than shrinking it.
insights.speaker: Adam Morgan
insights.so_what: Platform content-acquisition budgets, not consumer spend, were the marginal buyer of mid-budget games; track Game Pass and PlayStation first-party spend as the swing variable for indie studio survival.
insights.quote: Xbox Game Pass, PlayStation, and publisher funding were propping that middle space up, but most publishers have pivoted toward much smaller budgets.
insights.locator: The space between $2 million to $15 million

insights.claim: Publisher strategy has shifted from underwriting mid-budget bets to buying many cheap lottery tickets in hopes of another breakout like Balatro — a deck-building roguelike built by a single developer in his spare time that was profitable within 60 minutes of release and sold more than 5 million copies in its first year.
insights.speaker: Adam Morgan
insights.so_what: Publisher portfolios are becoming venture-shaped power-law bets; expected value per title falls while variance rises, which favors distribution and marketing platforms over content financiers.
insights.quote: Rather than going for mid-budget games, right now publishers are just pulling the slot machine a bunch of times and hoping they get another Balatro.

insights.claim: The window for double-A funding closed within a span of a few years, not gradually — a project that would have been a 'no-brainer' to fund shortly earlier came back from two industry conferences with nothing.
insights.speaker: Adam Morgan
insights.so_what: Studio business plans written pre-2022 are structurally obsolete; assume any independent developer without an owned back catalog is undercapitalized.
insights.quote: But funding for double-A games has evaporated.
insights.locator: If we were pitching that game just a few years earlier

insights.claim: Cyan Worlds spent four months building a fully playable demo, pitched more than a dozen publishers at GDC and the D.I.C.E. Summit seeking $1 million to $10 million, was positively received by most of them, and still secured no funding — demonstrating that demo quality no longer clears the greenlight bar.
insights.speaker: Adam Morgan
insights.so_what: Development spend on pitch material is now a sunk-cost trap for independents; the binding constraint is publisher balance sheets, not product risk.
insights.quote: Even the publishers who felt passionate about the project couldn't get their higher-ups to let the money flow,

insights.claim: The funding failure translated directly into headcount: Cyan put Anglerfish on ice and laid off 12 people, roughly half its staff, despite having a D.I.C.E. Award nomination for Outstanding Achievement in Game Direction for its Riven remake the same cycle.
insights.speaker: Adam Morgan
insights.so_what: Critical acclaim provides no financing buffer in this cycle — award recognition and layoffs are now coincident, not contradictory, indicators.

insights.claim: Cyan's survival strategy is to trade scope for solvency: the studio says it remains in good financial shape on the strength of its back catalog and has pivoted to a smaller-scale Myst-universe game codenamed Mudfish while predicting broad studio closures across the industry.
insights.speaker: Adam Morgan
insights.so_what: Owned IP back catalogs are the only durable balance sheet in independent games — a consolidation-of-catalogs thesis, not a consolidation-of-teams one.
insights.quote: We’re going to see a lot more studio closures in the future as a result of this funding issue, but Cyan won’t be one of them.
insights.locator: At Cyan, development director Hannah Gamiel

themes.theme: Discovery layer degraded by AI slop

insights.claim: More than 18,000 games on Steam now carry AI usage disclosures according to the AI Transparency Index, and the resulting flood of low-quality titles has eroded storefront curation as a discovery mechanism.
insights.speaker: Adam Morgan
insights.so_what: Generative AI is deflating the cost of supply faster than it improves it, transferring value to whoever solves discovery — a bullish setup for curation, creator brands and paid UA, bearish for storefront-dependent studios.
insights.quote: User trust in platform stores as a curatorial layer has been all but erased,

insights.claim: Lost discoverability compounds the funding problem: because standing out now requires additional marketing spend on top of development cost, publishers become even less willing to back mid-budget titles.
insights.speaker: Adam Morgan
insights.so_what: Marketing cost inflation raises the effective breakeven for every mid-budget game — model UA spend as a rising share of total project cost when underwriting studios.
insights.quote: When you feed people enough ads and slop, they just check out.

insights.claim: Practitioners see large corporations pursuing AI-generated entertainment as a separate track disconnected from working developers, while remaining optimistic about the quality of people and games in the independent space.
insights.speaker: Adam Morgan
insights.so_what: The AI content thesis in games is being pushed top-down by incumbents rather than pulled by creators — a signal that adoption may stall at the slop tier rather than move up the quality curve.
insights.quote: The large corporations just want some sort of AI-generated entertainment solution that has nothing to do with us,
insights.locator: Still, many indie developers are hopeful

insights.claim: Crowdfunding via Kickstarter, Indiegogo and Patreon rarely exceeds $1 million, which is an order of magnitude short of what a production like Anglerfish requires — meaning crowdfunding cannot replace the vanished double-A tier.
insights.speaker: Adam Morgan
insights.so_what: Don't model crowdfunding as a substitute for publisher capital above the $1M line; it is a marketing and validation channel, not project finance.
insights.quote: A million dollars seems like a ton of money, but it doesn't even come close to covering the full cost of a production like Anglerfish.

insights.claim: A new class of dedicated game funds — Outersloth, Blue Ocean Games and Midgame Fund — is emerging as the replacement for traditional publisher deals, but only for projects that stay inexpensive.
insights.speaker: Adam Morgan
insights.so_what: Watch these funds as the emergent financing layer for independent games; their check sizes will define the new ceiling on non-triple-A ambition.
insights.quote: The big publisher deals do feel like they’ve gone away, so you just have to look at more nontraditional routes,
insights.locator: Another Myst-influenced game with a mid-market budget

insights.claim: Successful independents are now inverting the pitch sequence — Blue Prince was funded entirely by its solo developer's personal savings and ad revenue from his Magic: The Gathering website, with publishers approached only after completion for marketing, porting and release support.
insights.speaker: Adam Morgan
insights.so_what: Publishers are being demoted from financiers to service vendors; the economics of a hit increasingly accrue to the developer, which is bearish for publisher margin capture on breakout titles.
insights.quote: When I finally approached publishers, it was only after I had completed my game, looking for marketing, porting, and release support,
insights.locator: Last year's indie darling, the Myst-inspired Blue Prince

insights.claim: Developers are deliberately capping ambition to preserve independence, explicitly trading loftier creative scope for the avoidance of a funding deal that would hand outside parties control over them.
insights.speaker: Adam Morgan
insights.so_what: Expect a persistent supply gap in cinematic, high-production-value non-triple-A games — the aesthetic category Myst defined is now economically unavailable, not merely unfashionable.
insights.quote: I'm going to keep my aspirations and scope rather small, because the last thing I want to do is put myself in a position where I have to make a deal that gives people power over me,
insights.locator: Ros says Myst and its first sequel Riven
